planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Jonathan requires roughly 700-800 chill hours and cross-pollination from a compatible variety such as Golden Delicious or Winesap, and is best adapted to zones 4-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Jonathan was discovered as a chance seedling in Woodstock, New York in 1826 and went on to become one of the most widely planted apple varieties in American history, remaining a dominant commercial and home-orchard apple for over a century. The medium-sized fruit ripens to a bright red over a yellow background, with crisp, juicy, aromatic white flesh balancing bright tartness with real sweetness, excellent for fresh eating, sauce, and pie alike. Jonathan is also historically significant as a parent variety, having been crossed with Golden Delicious to produce the modern Jonagold. Harvest when fruit colors fully and separates easily from the spur with a gentle twist, and note that Jonathan is somewhat more prone to bitter pit and early softening in storage than some modern keeper varieties, so plan to use it within a few months of harvest.

common_name: Cameo Apple (Modern Crisp Sweet-Tart Washington Discovery)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Cameo requires a compatible pollinizer variety and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Cameo was discovered as a chance seedling in a Washington State orchard in the late 1980s, believed likely to be a cross involving Red Delicious, and quickly rose to commercial prominence through the 1990s and 2000s for its exceptional eating quality. The medium-to-large fruit has a distinctive appearance, with soft red stripes over a cream to pale yellow background, and the dense, crisp, juicy flesh delivers a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up impressively well in cold storage, often improving in flavor after a few weeks. Cameo is a strong all-purpose apple, equally good fresh, in salads, or baked, and its firm texture and good keeping quality make it a satisfying choice for home orchards wanting a reliable modern variety alongside older heirlooms.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin requires a compatible pollinizer variety, needs substantial winter chill, and is best adapted to zones 4-7.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Baldwin originated in Massachusetts in the late 1700s and went on to become the single dominant commercial apple across New England through most of the 1800s and into the early 1900s, prized for large, firm, red-blushed fruit with crisp, juicy, slightly tart flesh that stores exceptionally well and holds up beautifully for baking, sauce, and hard cider alike. Baldwin's commercial dominance ended abruptly after the catastrophic winter of 1933-34, when extreme cold killed a huge share of New England's Baldwin trees, prompting growers to replant with hardier varieties like McIntosh; the apple never fully regained its former commercial standing, though it remains treasured by heirloom orchardists and cider makers. Harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and expect flavor to improve somewhat with a few weeks of cold storage, a classic trait of many old New England keeper apples.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Idared was bred at the University of Idaho and released in 1942 from a cross of Jonathan and Wagener, developed specifically to combine good eating quality with truly outstanding long-term storage life, and it remains one of the best-keeping apples widely available, often holding good quality for six months or more in cold storage. The bright, uniform red fruit has firm, crisp, white flesh that starts out notably tart and mellows into a pleasant, mild tartness in storage, making it a favorite for pies, sauce, and baking, since it holds its shape well under heat. The tree is vigorous, productive, and reliable, and the fruit's long shelf life makes it an especially practical choice for home orchardists wanting apples that last well into winter without special storage facilities.

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Wealthy is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating harsh northern winters, and is best adapted to zones 3-7.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing a compatible pollinizer variety nearby. Wealthy was bred by Minnesota horticulturist Peter Gideon in 1868 from a seedling grown from Siberian crabapple stock, and its success proved for the first time that quality apples could be reliably grown in Minnesota's harsh climate, making it foundational to the entire Northern apple-breeding tradition and a direct or indirect parent of many later cold-hardy varieties. The medium-sized fruit has red-striped skin over a pale yellow-green background and crisp, juicy white flesh, sometimes streaked with red, carrying a bright, tangy-sweet flavor good for fresh eating, sauce, and baking. As one of the hardiest widely available apple varieties, Wealthy is an excellent choice for northern growers, though it also performs reliably across a broad range of climates; fruit ripens in late summer to early fall and is best used within a few months, since it is not a particularly long-keeping variety.
